metadata.description:
Representational Falsification: A General Scientific Framework for Testing, Correcting, and Retiring Proxy‑Based Decision Systems

DESCRIPTION

Representational Falsification is an SR scientific‑governance mechanism that defines how institutions should test, challenge, correct, narrow, subordinate, suspend, or retire representations—scores, categories, dashboards, models, files, and algorithmic outputs—when adverse evidence shows that their authority no longer matches the governed condition.

The field introduces:

  • the representation‑use pair as the unit of adjudication

  • independent reconstruction of the represented object

  • severe testing designed to defeat the representation’s claim

  • rival representations and negative cases

  • transport tests across populations, horizons, and environments

  • authority consequences tied to failure

  • verification against independent outcomes

  • a graded verdict ladder (retain → monitor → recalibrate → narrow → subordinate → suspend → retire)

Representational Falsification distinguishes:

  • limit disclosure (scientific caveats)

  • limit preservation (self‑sealing disclaimers that protect authority without correction)

It provides a nine‑stage protocol, twelve hypotheses, comparative designs, and rejection conditions for the framework itself.
It is linked to Representational Displacement, Ground Truth Discrepancy, and Infrastructural Epistemic Lock‑In.

HOW IT CONTRIBUTES TO SR

1. It gives SR a formal mechanism for defeating proxy authority

Representational Falsification is the first SR field that defines how a representation loses authority when evidence contradicts it.

It operationalizes:

  • independent reconstruction

  • severe testing

  • rival comparison

  • transport conditions

  • authority consequences

  • post‑change verification

This is SR’s representational correction engine.

Linked concept: Scientific Demotion

2. It solves the institutional paradox: authority without corrigibility

Institutions often retain representations even after:

  • drift

  • misclassification

  • outdated assumptions

  • proxy substitution

  • verification closure

Representational Falsification explains why this happens and how to reverse it.

Linked concept: Verification Closure

3. It defines the representation‑use pair as the scientific unit

A representation is not valid “in general.”
It is valid for a specific use, population, horizon, and consequence.

This prevents:

  • global validity claims

  • universal authority

  • misuse across contexts

  • silent overextension

It is SR’s most important representational boundary rule.

Linked concept: Representation Use Claim

4. It introduces destructive testing as an epistemic discipline

Destructive testing is not sabotage.
It is a scientific procedure designed to defeat a representation’s claim under conditions where failure is informative.

This is SR’s severe‑testing architecture.

Linked concept: Severe Testing

5. It provides the authority‑consequence ladder

Representational Falsification defines the only SR ladder that connects evidence to authority:

  • retain

  • retain with monitoring

  • recalibrate

  • narrow

  • subordinate

  • suspend

  • retire

This ladder prevents symbolic audits and self‑sealing disclaimers.

Linked concept: Authority Consequence

6. It separates displacement from falsification

Representational Displacement diagnoses persistent proxy substitution.
Representational Falsification is the intervention discipline designed to defeat it.

This separation prevents SR from collapsing into a single mega‑construct.

Linked concept: Representational Displacement

7. It defines the representational chain and failure locations

The field maps the full chain:

world → observation → encoding → classification → aggregation/model → authorization → intervention → verification → revision

This allows SR to localize:

  • observation failure

  • encoding failure

  • classification failure

  • aggregation failure

  • model failure

  • authorization failure

  • intervention failure

  • verification failure

  • revision failure

It is SR’s most complete representational anatomy.

Linked concept: Representational Chain

8. It provides SR’s correction‑side falsification engine

Representational Falsification is the only SR field that:

  • defines correction latency

  • defines override executability

  • defines challenger influence

  • defines outcome improvement

  • defines revision history

It is the backbone of SR’s correction architecture.

Linked concept: Corrective Closure

9. It integrates with Institutional Coherence and Drift Dynamics

Representational Falsification explains how representations fail.
Institutional Coherence explains how execution fails.
Drift Dynamics explains how the substrate changes.

Together they form SR’s representational‑execution triad.

Linked concept: Institutional Coherence

10. It provides a general scientific governance mechanism

Representational Falsification is SR’s answer to:

  • model risk

  • indicator corruption

  • proxy dominance

  • self‑sealing disclaimers

  • representational drift

  • institutional opacity

It is the first cross‑domain mechanism that links evidence → authority → correction → verification.

Linked concept: Proxy Governance
